name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) hypertrophy

lead: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is the prominent muscle running from behind the ear down to the collarbone and breastbone on each side of the neck. Looksmaxxers build it to get a thicker, more defined neck.

The SCM rotates and tilts the head and flexes the neck, so training for it is generally discussed as resistance work for those movements. Anatomy sources describe the muscle's attachments, nerve supply and function; no study has examined deliberate SCM hypertrophy.

paras: People train neck rotation, tilt and flexion with resistance such as hands, bands or weights as part of a physique routine, combined with the diet and training that drive muscle gain elsewhere. Visible change in neck size generally takes months.
No cosmetic-specific risks are documented. Neck loading is generally regarded by clinicians as requiring care in people with cervical spine problems.

angle.text: Training the sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle on each side of the neck, grows it so the sides of the neck look thicker and more defined. The muscle's anatomy and function are well described.

lead: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is one of the largest and most superficial muscles of the neck, running on each side from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process behind the ear.[1] In looksmaxxing culture, "SCM hypertrophy" refers to building these muscles so the sides of the neck look thicker and more defined.

Anatomy sources describe the muscle's attachments, nerve supply and function, but the Wikipedia article does not cover training or hypertrophy.[1] No published study located for this article has examined deliberate SCM hypertrophy or its effect on appearance.
infobox: Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
Head rotation and tilt; neck flexion (both sides); accessory breathing

paras: The muscle has two heads, a sternal head from the upper front of the manubrium and a clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle, which merge into one rounded belly and insert on the mastoid process and the occipital bone.[1] The clavicular head varies in width between individuals.[1] It is clearly visible when the head rotates and forms a landmark that divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.[1][2]

Acting on one side it turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it toward the same side; acting together the two muscles flex the neck, and they help in forced inhalation as accessory breathing muscles.[1]
No studies found. Clinical literature on the SCM concerns conditions such as torticollis and its role in neurological examination, not cosmetic hypertrophy.[1]

The idea is discussed as part of neck development, alongside other neck-training topics, on the premise that a thicker neck contributes to a more imposing or masculine look. Anatomical sources note that average neck circumference differs between men and women and is attributed to muscle mass, BMI and testosterone.[2] No community sources were available to document specific protocols or claims.
